title: Fifty-Three Guineas
passage:
A subscriber to the book society had one volume out at a time and might keep it a fortnight. The second fortnight needed no asking. The mark cont. was written against the entry, and nothing was charged before the twenty-ninth day, when a penny a day began. What stopped the second fortnight was the slate by the door, where a subscriber set down the title he wanted; a volume so claimed came in on the fourteenth day. The slate was rubbed clean every week and no copy of it was kept. The shelves stood over a saddler’s shop in a market town twenty miles from navigable water, and the ledger ran from 1827 to 1835, every loan entered with its dates out and in, the volume and the name. Fifty-three subscribers paid a guinea a year, and three of them chose what was bought. A book of travels went out 41 times in those nine years; 39 of the loans came in on the fourteenth day, and two were continued. A volume of sermons went out nine times and was continued seven times. Ralph Jarrett, a currier, stood against more loans than any other name. Eleven of the fifty-three paid their guinea in each of the nine years and carried nothing home. A volume might be fetched by a servant or a child of the house, and the ledger named neither.
– Yvonne Hobbermarsh

questions.prompt: What can be concluded about the society’s subscribers?

options.text: Subscribers gave up the travels at the fortnight with another reader waiting for it.
Subscribers who kept the sermons past the fortnight paid a penny a day for them.
Subscribers settled at a meeting each year which new books the society should buy.
Subscribers who took no volume home stopped paying before the ledger’s last year.

questions.rationale: Option A is the answer, and the passage sets down the two facts that make it without ever joining them. The first is the society’s own rule. A second fortnight cost nothing and needed no application, so a borrower who wanted longer simply kept the book, and the one thing that brought a volume in on the fourteenth day was the slate, where another subscriber had set down the title. The second fact is the count: of 41 loans of the travels, 39 came in on the fourteenth day and two ran on. Thirty-nine borrowers over nine years gave up a free fortnight apiece, and under that rule the natural reading is that the title stood claimed while it was out. A is scoped to that and no further. It does not say the travels were the best-read book in the town, it does not say the borrowers had finished with them, and it does not name the readers who were waiting, because the slate that would have named them was rubbed clean each week and never copied. B is the fine misread, and it lives off the passage’s own words, since a penny a day is there and so is the fortnight; but the charge began on the twenty-ninth day, and the sermons were continued in seven of their nine loans without anything falling due. C is the outside-knowledge trap and the most respectable of the three, because book societies of the period did commonly vote their purchases at a general meeting; this one did not work that way, and the passage says in one clause that three of the fifty-three chose what was bought. D takes the sentence about the eleven who carried nothing home and attaches the obvious story to it, that a name with no loans against it belongs to a member who had drifted out of the society; the same sentence refutes it, since those eleven paid their guinea in each of the nine years. Every distractor turns on a clause a careful reader can point at, no distractor contradicts A, and no two options contradict each other, so no pair on the sheet advertises where the answer sits.

generator_meta.period_detail_note: Audited item by item against ordinary English book-society and subscription-library practice of the 1820s and 1830s. A guinea a year for a small-town society is in the normal range, and the guinea survived as a money of account long after the coin stopped being struck in 1816. One volume out at a time is the standard entitlement of a single share. A fortnight is a standard loan term for such a society. An overdue charge of a penny a day is at the low end of the usual penny-to-twopence range. Purchases chosen by a small committee of members, rather than by the whole subscription, is one of the two normal arrangements - the other, a general meeting that votes the year's books, is what distractor C offers and what this society is said not to do. A want list kept on a slate and rubbed out is an ordinary piece of counter equipment and an ordinary reason for such a list not to survive. Shelves in a hired room over a shop is the usual housing. WHAT A LEDGER WOULD AND WOULD NOT RECORD is the load-bearing period point and is handled explicitly: a borrowing register of this kind records the date out, the date in, a short title and the subscriber's name, and it does not record why a loan ended, who in the household read the book, or what stood on the want list - the passage says the last of these in terms and the closing sentence says the second. NO BOOK TITLES ARE PRINTED. The two books are named by kind ('a book of travels', 'a volume of sermons'), which is how a historian writes when the register's own titles are two or three words long; this borrows no real title and invents none, and so removes a law-16 surface rather than adding one. Both kinds are the right kinds: travels and sermons are the two commonest categories in surviving book-society catalogues of the period.
